Q: How to program a leaderboard with pygame? A:

You can use a dictionary with the player pseudo and their score or a list of tuple with their pseudo and scores: eg {sam:9, benoit:14} or [(sam,9),(benoit,14)]
Updating the scoreboard each time the score change is the best for a score based on events (eg: kills)

To sort the dictionary, i would convert it to a list of tuple, then sort the list of tuple with the itemgetter built in.

from operator import itemgetter

dict={sam:9, benoit:14}
list=[]
for key in dict:
    list.append(key,dict[key])

list.sort(key=itemgetter(1)) # 1 because it's the second element of the tuple that is the score

I think they're a better way to sort the dict.

Q: MySQL Group By: Select a single value from a group A:

If each document can have multiple files, but you only want one row per document, then you need a way to tell MySQL how to pick a single filename from each group.

Using ANY_VALUE() (when you truly don’t care)

If you simply want MySQL to return one filename from each group, and it doesn’t matter which one, you can use ANY_VALUE().

SELECT d.id,
       ANY_VALUE(f.filename) AS filename
FROM document d
LEFT JOIN document_file f 
       ON f.document_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id;

This tells MySQL: “For each d.id, just give me any filename from that group.”

It won’t randomly change every time you run the query, but you also don’t control which file is chosen. MySQL just picks one internally. This is the cleanest solution when the exact file doesn’t matter at all.

Q: Can you redefine the type of an object after the __init__ in python? A:

A couple of patterns here:

You can create a factory function

def create_item(name: str, amount: int) -> Item:
  if name == "hoe":
    return Hoe(amount)
  raise NameError(name)

create_item("hoe", 2)

You can similarly create a dictionary of names to their corresponding classes. In Python classes are callable (calling a class object returns a new object) and it can work to just say the dictionary values are just callable things.

from collections.abc import Callable

ITEMS: dict[str, Callable[[int], Item] = {
  "hoe": Hoe,
}

ITEMS["hoe"](2)

You can just store the name and type in the object and be done with it.

Item("hoe", 2)

If you go this last path, you get the question of "how do you have different behaviors for different types of objects?" You may want to ask this question even if you have separate classes. You can dynamically test this in the implementation

def on_right_click(item: Item):
  if item.name == "hoe":
    ...

(Imagine playing your game in a unit test, or over a remote ssh connection, or via an LLM; what does "right click" mean here? You could very readily want to separate the desktop UI from the core object model.)

You can't change an object's type in its __init__() method. In principle it would be possible from the class's __new__() but I'd generally discourage that: a base class shouldn't usually know what subclasses exist of it, if any.
